chunks: How to characterize a battery. The question: How do you characterize a battery?
To characterize a battery, treat it like any device under test and measure the numbers your design depends on.
The main ones are capacity, the voltage curve, internal resistance, self-discharge, and cycle life.
You repeat the tests at different currents and temperatures, because a battery's behavior changes a lot with both. Logging temperature the whole time is part of the job.
Think of testing a fuel tank. You fill it completely, then drain it at a steady rate while timing how long it lasts. That gives the capacity.
To see how clogged the nozzle is, you open the valve suddenly and see how far the flow drops. That is the internal resistance.
The picture has one gap: a battery's capacity also shrinks when you drain it fast or when it is cold.
A representative monotonic OCV curve (hand-built, not a datasheet).
It is steep near empty (below about 10%) and has a gentler slope through the middle; that is why a voltage-only fuel gauge is accurate near empty but coarse in the middle.
Capacity (Ah): the charge a battery delivers from full down to its cutoff voltage (the voltage at which it counts as empty).
C-rate: the discharge current relative to capacity, so 1 amps from a 2 Ah cell is 0. 5C. Open-circuit voltage (OCV): the cell's voltage after resting, with no load.
Internal resistance: the cell's own resistance, which makes its voltage sag under load. State of charge (SoC): how full the battery is, as a percent.
Charge a cell fully, let it rest, then discharge it at 1 amps until it reaches its cutoff voltage. Say that takes 2 hours. Then the capacity is 1 times 2 equals 2 Ah.
With an average voltage of 3. 7 volts, the energy is 3. 7 times 2 equals 7. 4 watt hours. For the resistance, apply a 1 amps pulse. If the voltage steps down by 0.
1 volts right away, then R equals 0. 1 over 1 equals 0. 1 ohms. That is the whole idea.
"I'd measure it like a device under test. Capacity: charge with CC/CV, rest, then constant-current discharge to cutoff and integrate current.
Open-circuit voltage versus state of charge, with rests, for the fuel gauge. Internal resistance from a current pulse: the instant voltage step over the current.
Then repeat across C-rates and temperatures, and measure self-discharge over weeks and capacity and resistance fade over cycling.
And I'd always record conditions, because every one of these numbers depends on rate and temperature."
